description: We are Team Calember. We love working with data from satellites. It's so fun. We are here doing what we love the most.
summary: Since 2000, MODIS sensors aboard NASA’s Terra and Aqua satellites have monitored active fires worldwide, but both satellites are drifting and expected to retire in 2027. Their replacements, VIIRS sensors, detect significantly more fires, creating an artificial jump of nearly 400% when their data is directly combined. Calember solves this through a machine-learning translator trained on overlapping MODIS and VIIRS observations from 2012–2019, converting VIIRS detections into MODIS-equivalent hotspots. Using 657.8 million NASA FIRMS detections, it creates a continuous, validated global fire record from November 2000 to the present. On unseen regions and years, Calember achieves a Kling–Gupta Efficiency of 0.9913, outperforming a lookup-table baseline of 0.9633. It reduces the artificial 2012 fire-count jump from 400% to just 4%, while a sensor-classification test achieves only 55% accuracy, indicating strong consistency with real MODIS data. The harmonized record is accessible through a free 3D interactive website, helping anyone explore historical fire activity and answer one important question: Is this month's fire activity normal for this place?
details:
GitHub Repo: https://github.com/Sandesh-077/Calember


The problem in one afternoon

On 7 November 2016, Aqua’s MODIS flew over Punjab and Haryana in India during the stubble-burning season and saw 922 fires. Minutes later, Suomi NPP’s VIIRS crossed the same fields and saw 8,206—same fires, same afternoon, 8.9 times the count.

VIIRS is not wrong. Its 375 m pixels are about seven times smaller than MODIS’s 1 km pixels, so it captures small fires that MODIS misses and splits large fires into several pixels. The ratio also changes from place to place, so no single number can undo it. Worldwide on 22 August 2019, the two sensors saw 12,118 and 58,496 fires.

This matters because the 26-year MODIS fire record is how scientists, governments and fire agencies answer a simple question: is this year worse than usual? MODIS is ending. Terra and Aqua have drifted off their original overpass times: Aqua from 13:33 to 14:47 local time, Terra from 10:34 to 09:22. Both end science operations in 2027. If the record cannot continue on VIIRS, the world loses its longest fire memory.

What we built

1. Calember, the record. A harmonized fire record covering:

  • 68.6 million cell-months;
  • 571,982 land cells of about 253 km² each (H3 resolution 5);
  • 313 months, from November 2000 to November 2026.

Every value is in one unit: hotspots (MODIS-equivalent), the number of cleaned detections that MODIS Collection 6.1 Terra + Aqua would have reported at their original, pre-drift overpass times. Each value comes with a 90 % range.

2. A website that makes it useful. It has three pages:

  • The story: a scroll-driven 3D film that explains the problem and the fix in a few minutes.
  • Calember Observatory: the main tool. A 3D night Earth with 26 years of fire and the five fire satellites in orbit.
  • The classic view: for screen readers and computers without 3D.

How the harmonization works

Step 1: Clean.

  • MODIS: we keep detections with confidence ≥ 30 and type 0 (vegetation fire).
  • VIIRS: we keep nominal- or high-confidence detections of type 0.
  • Static-source mask: gas flares and volcanoes are masked on a 5 km² grid. A cell is masked when VIIRS sees it in at least half of all months of 2013–2024, in at least 8 different years, or when any product flags it as a static source.
  • Why the mask is mandatory: VIIRS Collection 2 mislabels some gas flares as vegetation fires. The mask removes 60–76 % of detections in flaring regions such as the Persian Gulf and Khanty-Mansiysk, and under 2 % in farm and savanna regions.

Step 2: Describe. For every satellite, cell, and month, we compute a short description of what the sensor saw:

  • detection counts by day and by night;
  • fire radiative power (sum, median, 90th percentile, maximum);
  • pixel size and the share of weak fires;
  • the number of distinct fire days;
  • fire-cell-passes, our own measure. It counts how many separate “looks” saw fire, so the model can tell more fires apart from one fire seen as several pixels.

Step 3: Learn the translation on the overlap years. From 2012 to 2019, Aqua MODIS and Suomi NPP VIIRS cross the equator minutes apart in the early afternoon. Both answers are known for the same fires, so a model can learn MODIS’s count from what VIIRS saw.

  • Two models: gradient-boosted trees (LightGBM), one for Aqua and one for Terra, summed. They use a Tweedie objective and were tuned on an inner split only, never on the test sets.
  • Inputs: the cell’s VIIRS statistics, the six neighbouring cells, the previous and next month, the surrounding region (about 12,000 km²), latitude, season and biome. They also include the cell’s own history of MODIS against VIIRS, computed leave-one-year-out so a row never sees its own year.
  • Monotone constraints: the prediction can only rise when VIIRS sees more fire, so the model always behaves physically.
  • No leakage: training rows are chosen by “VIIRS saw fire” only. Choosing them by “any sensor saw fire” would quietly leak the answer into the training data.
  • Zero model: a separate model handles the case “VIIRS saw nothing here, but MODIS might have”.

Step 4: Uncertainty.

  • 90 % ranges: cross-fitted conformal prediction, calibrated separately for small and large counts.
  • Simulations: a zero-inflated negative binomial provides a full predictive distribution.

Step 5: Assemble one record. Each period uses the best source available:

Step 6: Repair sensor outages. Satellites go blind for days at a time.

  • Detecting a lost day: a sensor-day is “lost” when its global count falls below half of its 61-day median.
  • Filling it: lost MODIS days are filled from the paired satellite, and VIIRS inputs are scaled up for their lost days.
  • Tested: on 36 simulated outages, this fill brings the bias from −14.6 % to +0.1 %.
  • Flagged: every filled month is marked in the data.

How we proved it (scored only on data the model never saw)

We split the world into five folds of whole regions, so the model is always tested on places it was never trained on.

Development test: unseen regions, years 2018–2019. Higher is better.

Sealed 2020 test. We wrote it down in advance and ran it once: train on 2012–2019, predict 2020.

The second column exists because Aqua lost 80–95 % of its detections from 16 August to 2 September 2020. In those weeks, the “truth” itself has a hole, while Calember, built from VIIRS, keeps counting. We report 0.9684 as the headline score because it is the pre-registered one.

More tests:

  • The 2012 seam: after removing seasons, the jump when VIIRS joins falls from 399.5 % (raw) to 4.0 %. That is about as small as the 1.7–2.6 % we measure on placebo dates when no sensor changed at all.
    • Raw VIIRS: caught 77.4 % of the time.
    • Look-up table: 58.9 %.
    • Calember: 55.1 %, close to a coin flip (55.2 % on the sealed 2020 test).
  • Honest uncertainty: our 90 % ranges contain the truth 90.0 % of the time (89.7 % in 2020).
  • Matching the verdict: “Is this month normal?” verdicts agree with real MODIS at Cohen’s κ 0.473, against 0.347 for the look-up table.
  • Agreement before the drift: where MODIS is still trustworthy, annual totals for 2020 and 2021 match it at a ratio of 1.000.

The website: one question, any place on Earth

Choosing a place. Search, click, lasso or circle any area, type coordinates, or switch to a precise 2D map.

The seven stations. The chosen place lifts out of the globe onto a stage with seven stations:

  1. Verdict. Is this month normal? Live month-to-date from NASA FIRMS near-real-time data, a day-by-day chart, the month against every year since 2000, and a 90 % range.
  2. Terrain. Where inside the area it burns, cell by cell, month by month.
  3. Calendar. Every month since 2000 as a 3D landscape. Flip to “raw sensors” and watch the 2012 cliff rise, then collapse when harmonized.
  4. Season. When the fire season starts, peaks and ends, with trends and significance tests.
  5. Helix. 26 years in one spiral. You can listen to it.
  6. Twins. Places thousands of kilometres away that burn the same way, which you can fly to and compare side by side.
  7. Take it. CSV files, every single detection with its MODIS-equivalent weight, a ZIP bundle with metadata, and a 3D-printable fire calendar.

More pages.

  • Proof Lab: every benchmark above, visual and interactive.
  • Country rankings.
  • A playable Sensor Turing test: you try to spot the real MODIS record.

Hosting. The site runs for free with no server to keep alive. Named places come from precomputed files, and drawn areas are computed in the visitor’s browser by a JavaScript port of our Python API, parity-tested field by field.

Benefits and intended impact

  • The 26-year fire record survives MODIS. Fire trends, fire-season studies, and climate indicators keep a consistent baseline into the VIIRS era.
  • A fair comparison across 2012. Fire agencies and researchers can ask whether 2025 was worse than 2005 and get a fair answer.
  • One click, any area. Anyone, from a farmer in Punjab to a journalist or a land manager, can see whether this month is normal for their place.
  • Open and reproducible. The full method and the scripts to rebuild every step are in the repository.

What makes it creative

  • A Turing test for satellites. We judge success by whether a machine, or you, can still tell which sensor made the record.
  • A science film, not a slide deck. It shows a real afternoon through two satellites’ eyes: the Punjab dive, then the moment the 2012 cliff collapses. The score is synthesized live; MODIS has a woody voice and VIIRS a glassy one, and they slide into unison as the record is harmonized.
  • Your place on a stage. The chosen place lifts out of a 3D planet, with fire twins across the globe, sonification, and a fire calendar you can 3D-print and hold.

Factors we considered

  • Honesty over hype. No “100 %” claims, a sealed test run once, uncertainty on every number, and flags on filled, provisional, and drift-affected months. Every number on the site comes from our data files.
  • Pitfalls that break naive methods. We handled data leakage, gas flares mislabelled as fires, satellite orbit drift, sensor outages, and the end of Suomi NPP fire production.
  • Accessibility. A screen-reader-first classic view, reduced-motion support, keyboard shortcuts, and layouts that work on phones.

Tools we used

  • Python 3.12: Polars, DuckDB, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, LightGBM, H3, GeoPandas, Shapely, and FastAPI, tested with pytest.
  • TypeScript and React 18: three.js / React Three Fiber, MapLibre GL, D3, Tone.js and the Web Audio API, built with Vite.
  • Hosting: Cloudflare Pages, with Pages Functions and D1 for the live FIRMS relay and the Turing test scores, and a public Hugging Face dataset for the 657.8 million detections.

Known limitations

  • Calember reproduces what MODIS would have counted. It is not burned area or fire size.
  • Quiet off-season months in small regions are the hardest case.
  • June 2001 (Terra only, half the month lost) remains about 25 % low and is flagged.

The newest months use near-real-time data and are marked provisional.

Note: SI tools were used to assist with coding, debugging, data analysis, writing, and visual design, helping us bring our ideas to life and work more efficiently. All SI-generated outputs and information were thoroughly reviewed, tested, and reverified by team members to ensure accuracy, reliability, and quality.
